title: Polar coordinates
log: 2026-11-01T08:04:35Z match: Claude Haiku 5.5 found no bank point the same, so it is written new

match.reason: None of the bank points teaches polar coordinates; the closest, the unit circle card, covers only radius-1 cos and sin and does not introduce a general distance r from the origin, so a new point is needed.

draft.title: Polar coordinates
card: A point can be given as (r, θ). r is its distance from the origin. θ is the angle measured anticlockwise from the positive x-axis.
x = r cos θ and y = r sin θ. For (4, 60°): x = 4 × 1/2 = 2 and y = 4 × √3/2 = 2√3. The point is (2, 2√3).
r = √(x² + y²) and tan θ = y/x. Check which quadrant the point is in, because tan θ gives the same value in two opposite quadrants.
For (−3, 3), r = √(9 + 9) = 3√2. The point is in the second quadrant, so θ = 135°, not 45°.
draft.remember: x = r cos θ, y = r sin θ, and r = √(x² + y²). Use the quadrant to choose θ.

a.q: A point has polar coordinates (6, 30°). What is its y-coordinate?
a.why: y = r sin θ = 6 × sin 30° = 6 × 1/2 = 3. The value 3√3 comes from using cos 30° instead, which is the formula for x.

b.q: A drone is at the point (−2, −2) on a grid, with the origin as the centre. Which polar coordinates give its position?
b.why: r = √(4 + 4) = √8 = 2√2. The point is in the third quadrant, so θ = 180° + 45° = 225°. Using 45° ignores the quadrant, and 8 forgets the square root.
b.clue: Both coordinates are negative, so which quadrant is the point in?

final.title: Polar coordinates
card: A point can be given as \((r, \theta)\). \(r\) is its distance from the origin. \(\theta\) is the angle measured anticlockwise from the positive x-axis.
\(x = r\cos\theta\) and \(y = r\sin\theta\). For \((4, 60^{\circ})\): \(x = 4 \times \frac{1}{2} = 2\) and \(y = 4 \times \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = 2\sqrt{3}\). The point is \((2, 2\sqrt{3})\).
\(r = \sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2}}\) and \(\tan\theta = \frac{y}{x}\). Check which quadrant the point is in, because \(\tan\theta\) gives the same value in two opposite quadrants.
For \((-3, 3)\), \(r = \sqrt{9 + 9} = 3\sqrt{2}\). The point is in the second quadrant, so \(\theta = 135^{\circ}\), not \(45^{\circ}\).
final.remember: \(x = r\cos\theta\), \(y = r\sin\theta\), and \(r = \sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2}}\). Use the quadrant to choose \(\theta\).

a.q: A point has polar coordinates \((6, 30^{\circ})\). What is its y-coordinate?
a.why: \(y = r\sin\theta = 6 \times \sin 30^{\circ} = 6 \times \frac{1}{2} = 3\). The value \(3\sqrt{3}\) comes from using \(\cos 30^{\circ}\) instead, which is the formula for \(x\).

b.q: A drone is at the point \((-2, -2)\) on a grid, with the origin as the centre. Which polar coordinates give its position?
b.why: \(r = \sqrt{4 + 4} = \sqrt{8} = 2\sqrt{2}\). The point is in the third quadrant, so \(\theta = 180^{\circ} + 45^{\circ} = 225^{\circ}\). Using \(45^{\circ}\) ignores the quadrant, and 8 forgets the square root.
b.clue: Both coordinates are negative, so which quadrant is the point in?
